text: Rats, vacuums and pudding are funny. This one isn't.

For years, one of America's biggest banks told everyone to watch one number: how many products each customer had. The CEO's goal was eight per customer. Senators later quoted his line: "eight is great."
Employees had daily sales targets, and bonuses tied to them. So some of them did the cheapest thing that made the number go up.
They opened accounts customers never asked for. Checking accounts. Savings accounts. Credit card applications. Sometimes with fees the customer then paid.

In 2016, regulators fined Wells Fargo 185 million dollars. The bank's own count: about two million accounts that may not have been authorized. A year later, a bigger review raised it to about 3.5 million.

The regulator's director said it plainly: employees "secretly opened unauthorized accounts to hit sales targets and receive bonuses." Around five thousand three hundred employees were fired. In 2020, the bank agreed to pay three billion dollars to settle with the Justice Department and the SEC — which said the famous number investors watched had been inflated by unused, unneeded or unauthorized accounts.
The bank wanted loyal customers. It paid for accounts. So it got accounts.
